title: Risk-control matrix and expense claims
minutesWhy: The law row for this level (V3-STRUCTURE 3.3, Internal audit 2) fixes the work at 40 claims tested against a policy grid. A careful first-timer on a phone takes about 55 minutes over the RCM, the 40 claims, the recovery sheet and the four questions (designer round 2: 47 to 64), so the level shows 55, the honest time (house rule 1), above the SPEC 3.2 range of 15 to 40.

How to test travel claims against a grade and city grid
How to tell a design gap from a control someone skipped

Trace the breaches back to the controls

case.role: First-year article assistant on the internal audit team
case.client: Khamang Foods Private Limited, a Ranjangaon company that makes namkeen and chikki. Its board appointed our firm as internal auditor for 2026–27. About 140 of its 620 staff sell in the field.
case.team: Sameer Kulkarni (internal audit senior) and you; Jyoti Pingle, who leads accounts payable, runs the claims desk
case.goal: Document the controls over travel claims in a five-row risk-control matrix, test 40 claims against the policy and work out what to recover.
case.where: Accounts office, Ranjangaon plant · Monday 8 February 2027

messages: Morning. Travel claims at Khamang today. Build the five-row RCM from my walkthrough note first, then test my 40 picks against their policy.
Work out what to recover, claim by claim. All of it to me by 5, please. The closing meeting with Ashwin, their CFO, is on Thursday.

documents.subject: Travel and expense policy (extract)
body: ## 1. Grades
G1: sales officers and executives. G2: area sales managers and assistant managers. G3: regional managers and managers. G4: heads of department and above.
## 2. City classes
Class A: Mumbai, Pune, Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Delhi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Kolkata.
Class B: Nagpur, Nashik, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, Panaji, Vadodara, Surat.
Class C: every other place.
## 3. Hotel and daily allowance (₹)
Hotel, per night, taxes included:
Daily allowance (DA), per day:

DA is paid for each day away from the headquarters city on company work, the days of going and coming back included. It covers meals and small expenses and needs no bill. It is not paid for a day spent in the headquarters city.
G4: hotel and meals at actuals, with the CFO’s approval in the ERP.
## 4. Travel
- G1: train (AC 3-tier) or bus. G2: train (AC 2-tier) or bus. G3: train (AC 2-tier) or bus, or economy air for a trip over 500 km. G4: economy air.
- Own vehicle, on the kilometres in the trip log: two-wheeler ₹4 a km for every grade; car ₹10 a km from G2 up. Below G2, a car trip is paid at the two-wheeler rate.
- Auto, taxi or local bus in and around the town visited: at actuals.
## 5. Claims
- Claim in the ERP within 30 days of the last day of the trip. A later claim is paid only with the CFO’s approval.
- Attach the original bill for every item of ₹300 or more. DA needs no bill.

- Travel on a Sunday or a company holiday needs the manager’s approval in the ERP before the trip. Company holidays from October to January: 2 October, 7–11 November (Diwali shutdown), 25 December and 26 January.
- One bill is claimed once. A shared room is claimed once, by the senior person.
- A meal with distributors or customers: at actuals, with the bill and the guests’ names.
- Not paid: alcohol, tobacco, fines and penalties, personal items, family members’ costs.
## 6. Approval
- The reporting manager approves each claim in the ERP. A claim above ₹25,000 also needs the National Sales Manager (sales staff) or the head of the department.
- Nobody approves their own claim. A head of department’s claims go to the Managing Director.

documents.title: Sameer’s walkthrough note · claims
documents.subject: How a travel claim moves (with Jyoti Pingle, Accounts, and Priyanka Salunkhe, HR)
body: - After the trip the employee keys the claim into the ERP’s travel module, with photos of the bills. The module fills in the grade from the HR master and the city class from its own city table.
- **Grade caps.** The module will not save a hotel or DA line above the grade’s limit for that city class. Own-car and two-wheeler rates are one figure each, for every grade.
- **Duplicate block.** The module refuses a bill number the same employee has already used in a claim.

- **Manager approval.** The claim goes to the reporting manager in the HR master. Priyanka says managers are told to check the dates and places against the tour plan keyed in before the trip, then approve. Above ₹25,000 it also goes to the National Sales Manager (NSM) or the department head.

- **Bill check.** The originals reach Accounts in an envelope with the claim number. Jyoti’s claims desk ticks each line against the original bill, or the trip log for an own vehicle, and puts the claim in Friday’s payment batch. A claim sent after 30 days stays out of the batch until Ashwin approves it as a late claim in the ERP.

- **CFO’s monthly list.** On the 5th of each month Accounts print a list of the last month’s claims above ₹25,000 and claims sent after 30 days. Ashwin reads it, writes his queries on it and signs it.
- **Policy sign-off.** Every April each employee signs the travel policy as read.
Settings print from IT on file. Picks for testing: my list of 40.

tasks.title: Build the risk-control matrix
tasks.prompt: Sameer’s walkthrough note says how a claim moves at Khamang. For each of the five risks, pick the control that answers it, say whether it is preventive or detective and manual or automated, and pick how you will test it. Your RCM goes to Sameer when you move on.

lockOnLeave.note: He reviews it before you test. You can’t change it after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Sameer. You can read your RCM but not change it.

hints: Preventive acts before the claim is paid; detective finds a problem after. If no person does it, it is automated.

options.label: Vouch paid claims to their bills
Rerun all claims for repeat bills

items.label: Row 1 · Money not spent
items.prompt: Risk: an employee claims an expense that did not happen, or more than was spent.
items.note: Row 1: Jyoti’s claims desk ticks every line against its bill or trip log before Friday’s batch. A person, before payment: preventive, manual. Test it by vouching paid claims to their bills; asking Accounts whether they check proves nothing.

items.label: Row 2 · One bill paid twice
items.prompt: Risk: the same hotel bill, ticket or receipt is claimed and paid twice.
items.note: Row 2: the module refuses a bill number the same employee has used before. No person, and before payment: preventive, automated. Look at the setting, then rerun the period’s claims yourself for repeats, across every employee.

items.label: Row 3 · Above the grade
items.prompt: Risk: a hotel or daily allowance is paid above the limit for the employee’s grade and the city.
items.note: Row 3: the module will not save hotel or DA above the grade’s limit for the city’s class. Preventive, automated. Test the setting itself: the limits and the city table against the policy. Vouching claims tests people, not the module.

items.label: Row 4 · Days not travelled
items.prompt: Risk: allowances are paid for days the employee did not travel, or for travel nobody approved.
items.note: Row 4: the reporting manager checks dates and places against the tour plan before approving. A person’s judgement, before payment: preventive, manual. Test it on claims: tour plan, days away, Sundays and who approved.

tasks.title: Trace the breaches back to the RCM
tasks.prompt: Before the closing meeting Sameer wants the breaches traced back to the RCM. Answer his four questions from the settings print, the policy and the claims.
hints: A design gap lets the problem through even when everyone does the job. An operating failure is a good control someone skipped.

questions.text: Faisal and Santosh were both paid for one shared room, though the module blocks repeat bills. What failed?
questions.sample: Why the shared room got through

options.text: The duplicate check had been switched off, so the module stopped looking for repeat bills this year.
options.why: The settings print shows it on. It did what it was built to do; it was built too narrow.

options.text: It looks only within one person’s claims, so one bill under two names gets through: a design gap.
options.why: Even run perfectly, it cannot see a bill in someone else’s claim. The fix is to check bill numbers across every employee.

options.text: Santosh should not have claimed it: as the senior he had to leave the shared room to Faisal.
options.why: The policy says the opposite: a shared room is claimed once, by the senior person. Santosh’s claim is the right one.

options.text: Nothing failed: the policy lets each person who shares a room claim the whole bill himself.
options.why: One bill is claimed once. Two claims for one room means Khamang paid for it twice.

questions.text: Nilesh’s and Swapnil’s Sunday allowances were approved by their managers. How do you record this against Row 4?
questions.sample: How to record Row 4 for the Sunday allowances

options.text: Row 4 is designed well but failed in operation: the managers approved without checking the dates.
options.why: A good control that someone skipped is an operating failure. Test more of their approvals before you call it a pattern.

options.text: Row 4 is designed badly: staff who work on a Sunday should always be able to claim its allowance.
options.why: Neither of them worked away from home that Sunday. And with prior approval, Sunday travel is paid.

options.text: No exception for Row 4: once a manager approves a claim, its allowances count as checked.
options.why: An approval shows the step happened, not that it was done well. Both claims show the Sunday plainly.

options.text: Row 3 failed instead: the module should have capped each Sunday allowance at the limit.
options.why: The amounts were within the limits. The question was the day, which no cap looks at.

questions.text: Akash’s Nagpur hotel and allowance were above the policy’s limits, yet the module’s grade cap let them through. Why?
questions.sample: Why the grade cap passed Akash’s Nagpur claim

options.text: Akash keyed the hotel under another head, so the cap on hotel lines never looked at it at all.
options.why: The claim shows it as Hotel. The cap did look, at the wrong limit.

options.text: The cap applies only from G2 up, so a G1 officer’s claim goes to the manager with no cap at all.
options.why: The settings print shows the cap on for every grade but G4, so G1 lines are capped too.

options.text: Deepak overrode the cap when he approved the claim, which the module lets any approver do.
options.why: There is no override in the settings and none on the claim. The limit applied was class A’s.

options.text: The module’s city table puts Nagpur in class A, so it used class A rates; the policy says B.
options.why: A set-up error: the cap worked from the wrong table. Every claim for Nagpur since 1 April needs a look.

questions.text: Deepak approved his own Bengaluru claim of ₹33,260. How could the module let him?
questions.sample: How Deepak could approve his own claim

options.text: As National Sales Manager he is the final approver of every sales claim, and that includes his own claims.
options.why: The policy says nobody approves their own claim; a head’s claims go to the Managing Director.

options.text: G4 claims skip the manager step because the CFO approves actuals, so his own click was enough.
options.why: Actuals need Ashwin as well, and the policy sends a head’s claims to the Managing Director.

options.text: His “Reports to” in the HR master is blank, so the module sent the claim to his own list.
options.why: Master data broke the control: with no manager set, the module falls back to the claimant. List every blank “Reports to” in the HR master and check those claims.

options.text: Ashwin approved it on paper first, and Deepak only pressed approve in the module for him.
options.why: Nothing on file shows a paper approval. Without the evidence, the approval did not happen.

passNeeds.note: Your RCM needs more right: the control, its type and the test for each risk.
You need more of the 40 claims right to pass: the call and, for an exception, what is wrong.

wrap.text: Eleven breaches in forty, and four of them come from how the module is set up. Those lead the report, because they repeat every month. I have already told Ashwin about the city table and the duplicate check.

wrapPartial.text: Eleven breaches in forty, four of them from how the module is set up. Check your claim calls against the Limits tab and the policy before anything reaches Ashwin.

wrapRetry.text: Take the city’s class from the Limits tab, not the claim print. Check each DA day against the days away, each approver against the employee and each own-vehicle line against its trip log. Any other item of ₹300 or more needs its bill. The RCM comes from my walkthrough note.

blocks.text: The April policy sign-off answers none of the five risks: it tells staff the rules and checks nothing.
The four set-up gaps: the duplicate check sees one person’s claims only; Nagpur sits in class A; the car rate is the same for every grade; and a blank “Reports to” sends a claim back to its owner.
Eleven in forty sounds like a lot, but I picked for risk, not at random, so never quote it as a share of all 1,186 claims. For the four set-up gaps we pull every claim since April.

principles: Build the RCM from what the client does, then test each control the way it runs: an automated one by its setting, a manual one on the claims it passed.
Test a claim against the policy, not against the class or limit the system printed.
A design gap fails every time; a control someone skips fails now and then. Fix the first by changing the control, the second with the people who run it.

My row: a hotel above the grade’s limit. The module will not save it: preventive, automated.
In the simulation I tested its city table against the policy; it had Nagpur in class A.

interview.q: How would you find duplicate expense claims?
interview.checking: Whether you have a method beyond scrolling, and treat a match as a lead.
outline: Put the period’s claims in one sheet and match bill number, date and amount across employees.
In the simulation one twin-room bill named two guests, and both had claimed it in full.
A match is a lead: I read both claims and the policy before calling one a duplicate.
